One bar, one home. **What it counts, committed:** a question is answered when `typeof ans.score === 'number'`. Marking a question **not applicable removes it from both the numerator and the denominator.** This is not a new definition — it is exactly `Result.answered / Result.scoreable` and exactly `SectionScore.answered / .total`, which the scoring engine already computes at every level. So progress and score never disagree, nothing new is computed, and the existing footer text (which the test asserts as `of ${TOTAL - 1}` after one n/a) stays literally correct. ``` The track is four segments, `flex-grow` set to each domain's question count, separated by 2px gaps — so the bar is a small map of the instrument rather than a single number, and you can see which quarter you are in. `.prog-track { display: flex; gap: 2px; height: 9px }`, `.prog-seg { background: var(--surface-2); border-radius: 999px; overflow: hidden; box-shadow: inset 0 0 0 1px var(--line) }`, `.prog-fill { display: block; height: 100%; background: var(--accent); transition: width .28s ease }`, and `.prog-seg.done .prog-fill { background: var(--good) }`. proposals.tradeoffs:
**The repaint has to be narrowed. That is the one non-cosmetic change, and everything else depends on it.** Today every score click runs `changed() → repaintApp() → paint()`, throwing away and rebuilding 4,049 nodes including 67 `<details>`. A sticky header, a persisted collapse state, a completion animation and surviving focus are all impossible against that. So `renderSubmit` gains a small painter registry — `{ toc, footer, sec: Map<string, fn> }`, each a closure over the handful of nodes it built — and score and n/a changes route through a new `onScoreChange()` that recomputes `score(rubric, a)` (a pure pass over 176 questions, sub-millisecond), then calls the local painters. About 60 nodes instead of 4,049, and focus stays on the button you clicked. The safety valve is one comparison: if `markingProblems(a).length` differs before and after, fall back to `repaintApp()` — which is exactly the case where the first score in a blank file flips the save gate, the behaviour `test/ui.mjs` already asserts. Evidence changes, file marking and lifecycle stage keep the full repaint. This follows a pattern the file already uses (`paintScores`, `paintChosen`, `paintOther`, `evidenceEditor`'s `paint`), so it is an extension of the house style, not a new architecture.

**Sections never auto-collapse.** `el('details', { open: ss.answered < ss.total })` is one clever line that produces the app's worst interaction bug: a section collapses under the cursor the instant its last question is scored (4,415px → 56px, the page shrinking by 4,359px while the scroll offset holds), and manually reopening it is undone by the next click anywhere on the page. Collapse becomes the user's decision, stored and persisted. Completion is signalled in the heading instead — `14/14`, a `✓`, a green bar. One `button.ghost.small` "Collapse answered sections" in the part head gives the old behaviour on demand, to anyone who wants it.

**A third sticky tier costs reading room.** Chrome (86px) plus the sticky section heading (~40px) plus the 90px footer leaves about 684px of a 900px viewport, against 714px today. Thirty pixels buys the thing she asked for twice. On a 768px-tall screen the `max-height: 800px` rule strips the heading to a 32px single line.

**The rail costs horizontal room, and only above 1080px.** 15rem of a 1220px page. Below the breakpoint nothing is lost — the rail becomes the sticky strip and the reading column is unchanged.

**What I am deliberately not building.** No per-section pagination — all of a domain's questions stay in one DOM, which keeps Ctrl+F working across 61 questions, keeps the domain printable in one pass, and keeps `qa('.question').length === expectedQs` passing. No search or filter box. No jump-to-next-unanswered button (the rail's counts already show where the gaps are). No second progress bar in the footer. No confirmation dialogs. No `aria-live` progress announcements. She said she does not want it overcomplicated, and each of those is a thing to learn rather than a thing to read.

**One thing gets slightly worse:** three nested grounds (`--bg` → `--surface` → `--surface-2` → `--surface`) is more visual layering than today's two, and layering done badly is what caused the blending in the first place. It works only because the alternation is strict — each level flips back — and because the gutter number and the hairline reinforce the same boundary. If it reads busy in the browser, the fallback is to drop the `.q-ans` fill and keep only its score-coloured left rule; the numbering, gutter and heading carry most of the separation on their own.

proposals.risks:
**Print.** Four of today's defects get fixed and one new risk appears. Fixed: section titles now print (they are an `h3`, not a hidden `summary`); the score now prints via `span.q-answer-print` built inside `paintChosen()` — "Score 7 of 10 — Scalable & Secure", or "Not applicable", or "Not answered"; the 11-rung ladder stops printing (`.ladder-box { display: none }`, which was costing roughly 40 pages); and `.marking-banner.print-only` is finally unhidden inside `@media print`, so the foot-of-page marking the code comment intends actually appears. The new risk is the tinted `.q-ans` printing as a grey slab, killed explicitly: `.q-ans { background: none !important; border: 0; border-left: 1pt solid #999; padding: 2pt 0 2pt 8pt }`. Two more rules are mandatory: `.card { break-inside: auto }` must replace today's `avoid`, which would fight a 4,400px section card, with `break-inside: avoid` moved down to `.q`; and `.sec-head { position: static !important; break-after: avoid }`, because Chrome has been known to duplicate stuck headers across pages, and because a heading stranded at a page foot breaks her own document rule. Today's `button { display: none !important }` becomes `button:not(.sec-toggle) { display: none !important }` or the section titles vanish again. A full 176-question printout is still 60–70 pages; that is inherent to the instrument, not to this design.

**Phone, down to 360px.** The rail becomes a sticky strip: progress block plus the `.stepper` at `auto-fit minmax(150px,1fr)` (which wraps to two or three rows on a phone, ~150px tall) plus the section list folded behind `.toc-toggle`. Combined with the chrome that is a lot of fixed furniture on a 640px viewport. Mitigation: under `max-width: 700px`, `.prog` drops to a single 9px track with the count inline (one 34px line), and `.stepper` becomes a horizontally scrolling flex row (`overflow-x: auto; scroll-snap-type: x proximity`) so the five domains stay on one 44px line. That is the standard mobile-tabs pattern. The `.q` gutter narrows to `2.2rem` and `.ev-row` already collapses at 620px. This is a desktop tool on a locked-down laptop; the phone case needs to be survivable, not good.

**Keyboard and screen reader.** The highest-risk piece is the roving tabindex: if `aria-checked` and `tabindex` drift apart the score row becomes untabbable, and it is the only control that matters. It must be exercised keyboard-only and under VoiceOver before shipping — Tab into the row, arrows across, Tab out, and confirm the group announces its name from the question heading. Second: the rail is a second `<nav>` and the header's `nav.path` currently has no accessible name, so both need `aria-label` or a screen reader reads "navigation, navigation". Third: anchor navigation needs `tabindex="-1"` on `h3.sec-head`, or Tab after a rail click returns to the rail instead of entering the section. Fourth: `role="progressbar"` deliberately has no live region, so a screen reader user gets progress only on demand — the sticky footer's `N of M answered` sentence stays as the redundant text path, which is why no bar goes down there.

**Colour.** No state is colour-only. The `.q-ans` left edge and the `.q-state` fill are score-coloured, but the score number is always present as text in the row and in `.chosen`, and the glyph differs by shape — empty dashed circle, check, en dash. Domain and section completion would otherwise be colour-only on the bars, so both gain a `✓` in their count.

**The measured `--chrome-h`.** If the rAF never runs — print, JSDOM, a JS error earlier in `paint()` — the static 88px fallback applies and sticky headers sit a couple of pixels off. Harmless. The real failure mode is the topbar wrapping around 520px wide, which changes the chrome height; the resize listener corrects it, but a wrap triggered by a font-size change without a resize event would not be caught.

**IntersectionObserver.** Unguarded, it throws in JSDOM and the whole UI suite dies. Guarded, its absence costs only the rail's "you are here" highlight; the sticky section heading still answers the question. It must be rebuilt on every submit paint, and the 20 observers it creates must be disconnected first or they accumulate one set per paint — a slow leak that would show up after a few hundred clicks.

**The quiet failure.** `openSections` keyed by `${domainId}/${sectionId}` will silently mismatch if Dan renames a section id, leaving sections stuck in whatever state the old keys implied. Storing `rubricVersion` alongside and dropping the record on mismatch is the fix, and it is two lines — but it is the kind of thing that gets left out and then confuses someone for an afternoon.

proposals.lens: Long-form government survey instrument. The reference set is the GOV.UK "task list" pattern, the Statistics Canada electronic questionnaire, the T1 return's "Step N of 7" spine with numbered lines, and a clinical intake form. What those instruments share is an assumption this app does not currently make: the person will not finish in one sitting, will be interrupted, and the primary failure mode is losing your place. So they all do the same four things. They number everything, so any question has an absolute address. They chunk into named, numbered parts and show the whole part list at all times, with per-part status. They give completion feedback per part, not only at the end. And they resume you exactly where you stopped rather than at the front door. This app currently does none of the four, which is why 176 questions read as one sheet.
proposals.summary: Turn the questionnaire into a numbered form with a permanent left rail: the rail carries the overall progress meter and a task list of the current domain's sections with per-section status, so the "tabs" she could not find are on screen at all times and cost no vertical space. Make the domain stepper sticky and compact so it pins under the header like a row of Excel tabs, add a 4px progress strip inside the existing sticky chrome block, and turn each question into a bordered card with a number in a left gutter, a status edge, and its answer controls inside a tinted answer box, so the section is a container of cards rather than 61 hairlines on white. proposals.tradeoffs:
**What this costs.**

The rail needs horizontal room. Below 1100px it has to leave the flow, so there are two layouts to maintain rather than one. The degradation is cheap and uses the same DOM: the rail becomes a `<details>` inside the sticky stepper block, its summary reading "Part 3 of 6 · Demonstrated Engagement · 6/9 ▾" in 32px, opening the identical `ol.rail-list` as a dropdown panel. Below 700px the stepper's five columns become a horizontal scroll strip, `overflow-x: auto; grid-auto-flow: column; grid-auto-columns: 8.5rem`, which is literally the Excel tab strip she described.

The sticky stack is now three deep on screen: chrome, stepper, section summary. Three is the practical ceiling and I have spent it. There is no room for a fourth, so any future always-visible element has to go in the rail or replace something.

One section open at a time means Ctrl+F across a whole domain no longer finds text in the other five sections. This is a real loss and worth naming to her. It is the price of not having a 20,190px page, and the mitigation is that the rail makes the other five reachable in one click, and the print view opens all of them.

Widening `.body` to 1200px on the submit view makes the questionnaire wider than the results and reviewer pages, which stay at 940px. That inconsistency is deliberate: the questionnaire is the only view with a rail.

`meta.place` puts a UI cursor inside the assessment file that gets emailed to TBS. Slightly odd, and the alternative is resume that breaks the moment she saves and reopens, which is the exact workflow the tool recommends. Keep the cursor.

**What I chose against.**

*One page per section, 21 pages.* This is what GOV.UK would do and it is the purest version of the chunking. Rejected on two grounds. It breaks `test/ui.mjs` in three places, including the walk that proves all 176 questions are reachable, and it turns four Next clicks into twenty. The accordion gets nearly all of the benefit, keeps every existing selector, and, because closed `<details>` children stay in the DOM, the test's `qa('.question')` count and its clicks on buttons inside closed sections keep working unchanged.

*Collapsing answered questions to one line.* Tax software does this and it would shorten the page a lot. Rejected because it is the same class of behaviour as the bug she is already annoyed by: content vanishing under the cursor. An answered question compacts visually and moves not one pixel.

*Zebra striping the questions.* Cheaper than cards and would work. Rejected because cards plus a number gutter plus a status edge give figure and ground, an obvious top edge, per-question status, and a print unit that can avoid a page break. Zebra gives one of those, and zebra combined with a tinted answer box goes muddy.

*Making the eleven score buttons real radio inputs.* Semantically correct and free arrow keys. Rejected because `<label>` has no `.disabled` and label-click forwarding in jsdom is unreliable, which breaks two live assertions. `role="radiogroup"` on the row with `role="radio"` and `aria-checked` on the existing buttons, plus roving tabindex and ArrowLeft/ArrowRight/Home/End that move and select per the WAI-ARIA pattern, gives the same semantics, the same arrow keys, and cuts the row from eleven tab stops to one. Tab stops per domain page drop from about 930 to about 340.

*A per-question comment or scroll-spy for the rail.* Both dropped as unnecessary once exactly one section is open.

**If time runs short, cut in this order.** The sticky section summary goes first; the rail already names the section. Then the section-completion sheen. Then the all-done glow. What must not be cut, because each one answers a complaint verbatim: question cards on a tinted section ground with a number gutter, the sticky stepper, the rail with its meter and section list, the accordion that never closes itself, and the narrowed repaint that makes the rest hold together.

Keyboard. proposals.tradeoffs:
**What the spreadsheet metaphor buys.** Orientation at all three levels at once, from three devices that each cost under 40px. A 5× shorter page. Eleven to twelve questions in the band instead of one. Scoring 61 questions with 61 clicks and no expansion. Tab stops per domain falling from 930 to about 185, because the strip is one radiogroup rather than eleven buttons. And a real heading outline — one `<h2>`, twenty `<h3>`, 176 `<h4>` — where today the entire Business page has a single heading and section titles are `<span>`s inside a hidden `<summary>`.

**What it costs, and I am not going to soften these.**

*No `<table>`, so no grid semantics.* A real table would let NVDA and JAWS announce column context and offer table navigation — but table navigation mode intercepts the arrow keys, which is exactly the gesture the score strip needs, and eleven buttons in one cell get read with the column header prepended on every focus move. The full-width drawer would need `colspan`; in grid it is `grid-column: 1 / -1`, free. So this is a list that looks like a sheet: `<ul class="rows">` of `<li>`, each an `<h4>` plus a `radiogroup`. A screen-reader user gets a clean 176-item outline and no grid navigation. That is the better trade for this content and I would make it again.

*No true one-line row.* Question text is 67 to 141 characters, median 116, so at a 642px text column most rows are two lines. A one-line row would mean truncating the question, which is the one thing on the page that must never be truncated.

*Arrow-to-select changes muscle memory.* Radiogroup convention is that arrowing moves *and* selects, so a keyboard user can no longer Tab straight onto segment 7 — they Tab to the strip and arrow across. Faster, conventional, and different from the current build.

*The metaphor over-promises.* Sheet tabs imply rename, reorder, add. None exist. Mitigated by giving the tabs no context menu, no `+` tab, no drag affordance, and `cursor: pointer` rather than `grab`.

*Two densities, one design.* Because the drawer is `hidden` rather than absent, DOM node count stays roughly what it is — it is *layout* that collapses, since hidden subtrees are not laid out. Combined with dropping 176 ladder copies, the Business page goes from about 4,049 nodes to about 2,280, which makes the remaining full repaints materially cheaper.

**What I rejected.** Sticky section headers as a third tier: 156px of top chrome is already 17% of a 900px viewport, and the frozen bar's active chip already names the section. A read-only dense grid alongside the editor: two renderings of the same 176 questions is the definition of overcomplicating it. A horizontally scrolling grid: dead on a trackpad, dead on print, dead for keyboard. Auto-collapsing a completed section: that is the current bug — a section shrinking from 4,415px to 56px under the cursor — and the fix is a stored `Set`, defaulting to all open, never closing itself.
