"a progress bar... make it sparkly... also needs to be always seen": PARTLY. Three grains, all pinned. But the 4px strip spans 176 questions, so one answer moves it 0.57% — invisible, which is the thing she asked to be able to see. The "sparkly" is a 12% overshoot on a tick glyph. Thin.

"i also dont wanna overcomplicate it": WORST OF THE FOUR. Its own text says "two focused days," "three is the practical ceiling and I have spent it," and it accepts losing Ctrl+F across a whole domain. It writes a UI cursor (`meta.place`) into the assessment JSON that gets emailed to TBS — Proposals 3 and 4 both keep view state in a separate localStorage key, which is the right call. Three breakpoints, two layouts, a three-method `Changed` interface. Excellent engineering, more than she asked for.

scores.lens: Proposal 2 — Spreadsheet taken literally (frozen header, row grid, sheet tabs at the bottom edge)
scores.note:
"it all blends into one vertical sheet": FIXED HARDEST. Five stacked separating devices where there is one 1px hairline today, and — the part that matters — the drawer removes blocks rather than fencing them. Business Architecture goes 20,190px to ~4,014px, one question in the usable band to eleven. Measured, credible.

"I wouldn't even know there are different tabs": FIXED BEST. Numbered section chips pinned in a frozen bar with scroll-spy highlighting, plus a column-header strip repeated once per section so a label is never more than 14 rows away. She cannot fail to see that sections exist.

"like in Excel, they would always be seen": LITERAL BUT RISKY. Sheet tabs bottom-left is genuinely Excel, and merging them into the existing sticky footer costs zero vertical space — clever. But it puts primary navigation at the bottom of a government form, sharing a 62px bar with a progress readout, Save, and See my results. Crowded, and unconventional for the web she works in.

"a progress bar... sparkly... always seen": FIXED WELL. The 600ms green row wash is the best-placed "sparkly" of the four — it happens where her eye already is. And the insight that a pinned chip means "the reward is visible no matter how far down the sheet she is" is the sharpest observation in the set.

"i also dont wanna overcomplicate it": FAILS. It rebuilds the eleven score buttons as a contiguous 11-segment fill strip (22 new colour rules) and changes selection to arrow-moves-and-selects. It deletes the per-question ladder — live guidance she reads while scoring — and replaces it with a hover hint, which is dead on touch. It breaks test line 151 (`qa('.question')[0].textContent.includes('Symbiotic')`), one of five test edits. Its own mobile section concedes "that is the metaphor breaking." The estimate of "about a day" is not consistent with the bill. Highest chance she looks at it and says this is not what I asked for.

scores.lens: Proposal 3 — Progressive disclosure as a workbook (21 stops, sticky domain tab strip, sticky section rail, two progress bars)
scores.note:
"it all blends into one vertical sheet": FIXED, and by the right mechanism. Three moves, in order of force: the page becomes 3 to 14 questions instead of 61, so there is no vertical sheet left to blend; each question becomes a white card on a grey ground with a number and a state rail; and the justification and evidence fold behind one labelled door ("Why, and evidence" with a state chip). That third move is the closest read of her actual sentence — she is describing too many peer-level blocks, and this is the proposal that REDUCES the block count per question from about five to two rather than drawing more lines between them. Card goes 310px to 195px, three in the band where one fits today.

"I wouldn't even know there are different tabs": FIXED DISPOSITIVELY. You cannot be unaware that other sections exist when you are only ever on one and the rail lists all of them with counts. Belt and braces: the section header also goes sticky below 1000px where the rail folds away.

"like in Excel, they would always be seen, so you know where you are": FIXED, and in the shape she named. 38px tab row inside the existing `.chrome` block, `border-radius: 8px 8px 0 0`, active tab painted `--surface` to match the page — that is the Excel convention of the live sheet being the tab that matches the sheet. It reuses the one sticky container whose stacking order main.ts already reasons about, so no new z-index tier appears. Costs 38px of a 900px viewport.

"a progress bar... make it sparkly... have an animation when you finish a question. But that also needs to be always seen": FIXED BEST, and it is the only proposal that thought about magnitude: "one bar over 176 questions moves 0.57 percent per answer, which no one can see, while the section bar moves 11 percent." Two bars in the sticky footer, and the animation belongs to the one that visibly moves. Six one-shot keyframes — button pop, the check drawing itself and staying as the permanent state marker, one ring off the card, a bar bump with a single sheen pass. "There is no perpetually animating bar in the corner of a government form" is the right instinct for a Protected B tool.

"i also dont wanna overcomplicate it": HOLDS UP, with one charge. I verified the zero-test-edit claim against test/ui.mjs and it survives: sections stay mounted with `hidden`, so `qa('.question')` counts hold per domain (textContent includes hidden nodes, and jsdom clicks buttons inside them), `.card.section` counts hold, `"5% of this domain"` is verbatim, `.stepper .step` stays 5 with buttons as direct children, and `.chosen`/`Symbiotic` stay inside the card. It uses no IntersectionObserver at all — current section is page state, not scroll-spy — which sidesteps the jsdom trap the other three have to guard. Diff is moderate: ~250 net TS lines, ~200 CSS, view state in a separate localStorage key so nothing UI-shaped rides in the file sent to TBS. The charge: 21 stops is a bigger behavioural change than she asked for, and `hidden="until-found"` plus `beforematch` is exotic machinery bought to paper over the Ctrl+F loss pagination causes. Defensible — one page per part of a form is the T1 and StatCan convention, and the sections are Dan's own weighted structure, not an invention — but it is the thing to check with her first.

scores.lens: Proposal 4 — The assessment as a published standard (1.1.4 numbering, TOC rail, sticky numbered section headings)
scores.note:
"it all blends into one vertical sheet": WEAKEST MECHANISM, SHARPEST DIAGNOSIS. It is the only proposal that names the actual cause in one sentence: "Today evidence is the only tinted block in the whole question, which is why it reads as the most important thing; flipping it puts the tint on the answering apparatus, where it belongs." That is correct — I confirmed `.evidence` is the sole tinted block inside a question (styles.css line 362) while questions are divided by `border-top: 1px solid var(--line)` on flat white. But then it KEEPS the hairline: `.q { border-top: 1px solid var(--line) }`. The question does not become a card. It relies on a 3.1rem hanging-number gutter, 1.2rem/1.4rem padding, and the tinted `.q-ans` panel. Its own tradeoffs section concedes "three nested grounds is more visual layering than today's two, and layering done badly is what caused the blending in the first place," and pre-plans a fallback. Retaining the exact device she is complaining about is the wrong bet on her loudest complaint.

"I wouldn't even know there are different tabs": FIXED, most literally of the four. A real sticky `h3` glued under the chrome means the section name is on screen for every pixel you read it. It also fixes four things at once — a real heading outline, a title that survives print, and the end of the derived-open-state bug.

"like in Excel, they would always be seen": PARTIAL MISS. It satisfies "always seen" but discards the shape she named — the five domains become a vertical list in a 15rem sidebar, then flip back to a horizontal strip below 1080px, so the layout she learns at her desk is not the one she gets on a smaller screen. It also stacks progress, five domains, up to six two-line section rows and a "you are here" line into one rail with `overflow-y: auto`, so on a 768px laptop the domain tabs can themselves scroll out of the rail. She said "I liked it how they were always seen."

"a progress bar... sparkly... always seen": FIXED. The four-segment track with `flex-grow` set to each domain's question count is genuinely good — the bar is a small map of the instrument, not just a number. But movement is still 1/176 per answer, and it is the only proposal with no second grain of bar.

"i also dont wanna overcomplicate it": BEST OF THE FOUR. Smallest diff, honest "about a day," zero test edits (and it is the only one to catch the `:first-child` trap — wrapping `button.step` in `<li>` would silently break test line 143), and an explicit list of what it refuses to build: no pagination, no search, no jump-to-next-unanswered, no second bar, no dialogs, no aria-live. That list is itself the correct answer to her sentence. If her first complaint were softer, this would win.

verdicts.winner: Proposal 3 — Progressive disclosure as a workbook (21 stops, sticky domain tab strip, sticky section rail, two progress bars)
grafts: From Proposal 4 — the evidence tint inversion, which is the sharpest read of her sentence in the whole set and Proposal 3 never states it. `.evidence` is currently the ONLY tinted block inside a question (styles.css:362), so the strongest boundary on the page sits INSIDE a question rather than between them, and the eye reads evidence blocks as the page's rhythm. Flip it: tint the answering apparatus, set `.evidence { background: var(--surface) }`. Proposal 3 folds evidence into its `q-more` drawer, but when that drawer is open its contents must not recreate today's problem — apply the inversion inside the drawer.

From Proposal 2 — the print mechanics for typed values, the one real defect none of the other three address. Form controls do not reliably print what was typed into them, so Proposal 3's printed assessment will show empty justification boxes. Mirror the justification into a `

` on the **`input`** event (not `change`, so a note typed and printed without leaving the field still prints), and carry the score as `data-print="7 / 10 — Scalable & Secure"` rendered with `content: attr(data-print)`, which needs no extra node. Also gate it: only drawers with content should print.

From Proposal 1 — the one-line fix for section titles vanishing on print, with its necessary partner. Today `@media print` sets `details > summary { display: none }`, which is why titles disappear; the reason it was written that way is that `details { display: block }` expands all 176 ladders. So `details > summary { display: block }` must ship together with `.ladder-box { display: none !important }`. Proposal 3 reaches the title half by using real headings, but the ladder kill is what makes it safe, and it is worth ~40 pages.

From Proposal 4 — `button:not(.sec-toggle) { display: none !important }` in print. Today's blanket `button { display: none !important }` is precisely why the score selector does not print. Any disclosure control built as a button must be exempted by name, or the fix regresses the moment someone converts a heading to a toggle.

From Proposal 4 — `.card { break-inside: auto }` as an explicit REPLACEMENT for today's `page-break-inside: avoid`, with `break-inside: avoid` moved down onto the question. A 4,400px section card can never honour `avoid`; a 195px question card can. Proposals 1 and 3 both put it on the question but leave the stale rule on `.card`.

From Proposal 1 — `scroll-margin-top` on every focusable target inside a section, not just the section anchors: the question, the textarea, the score row, the evidence block. Tab landing on an element scrolled under a pinned header is the classic sticky-nav keyboard bug, and browsers honour `scroll-margin` for focus scrolling, not only `scrollIntoView`. Proposal 3 adds a sticky tab strip and a sticky section header on narrow screens, so it owns this bug.

From Proposal 4 — the `h > 0` guard on the measured `--chrome-h`. All of Proposals 1, 2 and 4 measure chrome height into a custom property; only Proposal 4 guards it so jsdom (which returns zeros) stays on the static fallback instead of writing `0px` into every sticky offset.

From Proposal 2 — namespace every rubric-derived DOM id and storage key as `${domain.id}--${section.id}`, and sanitize with `s.replace(/[^A-Za-z0-9_-]/g, '_')`. I confirmed in the data that `defining-the-current-state` appears in all four domains — which is also the likeliest reason she read those section headers as mystery tabs. Proposal 3 keys its saved place by domain plus section, but the same rule has to cover ids and any collapse-state keys, and Proposal 4's point about dropping the record on a `rubricVersion` mismatch prevents a silent stuck-state bug if Dan renames a section.

From Proposal 1 — debounce the screen-reader progress announcement to about 600ms and say only the count, with a sentence on section completion. Proposal 3 announces section changes and completion only; adding a debounced count is better than either firing on all 176 clicks or staying silent.

From Proposal 2 — put the section-completion flash on an element that is PINNED, so the reward is visible however far down the page she is. Proposal 3's "Complete" badge sits in the section header, which is only sticky below 1000px; at desk width the reward can fire off screen. Move it to the rail row, or to the domain tab in the chrome.

From Proposal 4 — hand her the "what I am deliberately not building" list as part of the delivery. Given "i also dont wanna overcomplicate it," naming the four or five things that were considered and refused (no search, no jump-to-next-unanswered, no confirmation dialogs, no confetti) is worth as much as the build itself, and it is the cheapest thing on this list.

From all three non-winners — keep the classification marking as the ONLY hard gate, and say so out loud to Dan rather than leaving it as an omission. All four proposals independently reached it, all four correctly refuse to make justification or evidence mandatory across 176 questions, and all four keep the soft flag as a WORD rather than a colour. That unanimity is worth reporting as a finding.
verdicts.reasoning:
The brief says to weight "it all blends for me into one vertical sheet" highest and "i also dont wanna overcomplicate it" heavily, so I scored on mechanism strength against her five sentences and on diff size verified against the actual files, not on elegance.

The discriminator on her first complaint is a nuance in her own wording: "the evidence is a separate block, the questions is a separate block, but the whole thing just blends." She is not saying the blocks lack borders. She is saying there are too many peer-level blocks in a repeating unit, so no boundary reads as the important one. I confirmed the mechanism in styles.css: questions are divided by `border-top: 1px solid var(--line)` on flat white (line 320), while `.evidence` is the only tinted block anywhere in a question (line 362) — so the strongest visual edge on the page sits inside a question rather than between two of them. Proposals 2 and 3 answer that by REMOVING blocks (a drawer, a folded door). Proposals 1 and 4 answer it by adding a third nesting level with everything still on screen. Proposal 4 diagnoses her sentence most precisely and then keeps the very hairline she is complaining about, and concedes in its own tradeoffs that its layering could reproduce the problem.

Proposal 3 wins because it is the only one that gets all four of her concrete asks with the right mechanism and still keeps the bill small. Its page becomes 3 to 14 questions, which dissolves "one vertical sheet" structurally before any styling; it folds the exact block she named behind one labelled door; it puts the five domain tabs back in the shape she described, horizontally pinned at the top inside the sticky block main.ts already reasons about; and it is the only proposal that thought about how far a bar actually moves — "one bar over 176 questions moves 0.57 percent per answer, which no one can see, while the section bar moves 11 percent." That single observation is what makes her "make it sparkly" request satisfiable rather than decorative.

I verified its riskiest claim rather than taking it. Zero test edits holds: hidden sections keep `qa('.question')` counts intact because textContent includes hidden nodes and jsdom clicks buttons inside them without hit-testing; `.card.section` counts, the verbatim "5% of this domain" string, `.stepper .step` at 5 with buttons as direct children, and the per-question `.chosen`/`Symbiotic` assertions all survive. It also uses no IntersectionObserver — current section is page state — which avoids the jsdom guard that Proposals 2 and 4 both have to remember.

Against it: 21 stops is more behavioural change than she asked for, and `hidden="until-found"` with `beforematch` is exotic machinery bought to offset the find-in-page loss that pagination causes. That is the one thing to put to her before building, and it is the reason I scored it 9 rather than higher. Proposal 4 came second because it is the most disciplined and the safest, and it would win outright if her first complaint were softer; its grafts — especially the tint inversion — are what close Proposal 3's remaining gap. Proposal 1 is the strongest engineering document and the most over-scoped, spending its whole sticky budget, losing Ctrl+F, and writing UI state into the file that goes to TBS. Proposal 2 has the best density, the best print mechanics and the best insight about pinned rewards, but it rebuilds the score control, deletes the per-question ladder she reads while scoring, and its own mobile section admits the metaphor breaks — the highest risk of a "this is not what I asked for" reaction from someone who values conventions over invention.

scores.lens: The assessment as a published standard (numbered outline + TOC rail)
scores.note:
Highest implementation care of the four, by a clear margin, and the only one I believe on cost (~1 day, 4 files, additions-only tests).

VERIFIED CORRECT: (1) It is the only proposal that catches why wrapping the stepper buttons in <li> would break `qa('.stepper .step.complete:not(:first-child)').length === 4` — each button would become its own :first-child. It keeps nav.stepper byte-for-byte for exactly that reason. (2) It is the only one that keeps BOTH classes on the question node (`class="question q t7"`) specifically so `qa('.question')` needs no test edit. (3) It guards IntersectionObserver AND names jsdom as the reason — jsdom 29.1.1 has no IO, confirmed. (4) It guards the chrome measurement with `if (h > 0)` and names jsdom returning zeros — `getBoundingClientRect().height` is 0 there, confirmed. (5) It uses real `<a href="#…">` anchors, so it never touches `scrollIntoView`, which is undefined in jsdom. (6) It re-checks `markingProblems(a).length` before/after a score and falls back to the full repaint when it flips. That is load-bearing: `hasContent` in marking.ts includes `typeof ans.score === 'number'`, so the first score in a blank file arms the save gate. Without that valve the Save button goes stale and an unmarked Protected file becomes saveable. (7) Print: it catches that `.card { page-break-inside: avoid }` must become `auto` with `avoid` moved down to the question, that `.marking-banner.print-only` is never overridden inside @media print, and that today's `button { display: none !important }` would hide its own new section-toggle buttons. (8) It defaults every section open, so the suite's 176-question walk stays a walk over visible nodes.

DESIGN JUDGEMENT: inverting the evidence tint is the sharpest observation in any of the four. `.evidence` is genuinely the only tinted block inside a question today (`--surface-2` on white, styles.css:362), which is exactly why evidence reads louder than the question — verified. Putting the tint on the answering apparatus and flipping evidence back to `--surface` is the direct fix for her wording. And it names its own escape hatch if three nested grounds read busy: drop the `.q-ans` fill, keep the score-coloured left rule.

COSTS I AM MARKING IT DOWN FOR: it does not shorten the page at all — Business Architecture stays ~20,000px, and it rejects pagination outright. Its vertical stepper in the left rail is the weakest answer to "like in Excel, they would always be seen"; she pictured a pinned row of tabs, and a vertical list in a margin is not that (it restores a horizontal row only below 1080px, which inverts the priority). And 1.1.4 is an invented address sitting beside `BU-Q29`, which is two numbers per question in a tool whose output gets read against Dan's workbook. Its overall bar also moves 1.6% per answer in Business, better than 0.57% but still not the visible reward she asked for.

scores.lens: Long-form government survey instrument (task list + numbered form)
scores.note:
The best-grounded design decisions of the four, undone by two concrete day-one defects.

BEST IDEAS, VERIFIED: (1) Making `nav.stepper` sticky is a pure-CSS change on unchanged DOM. `.stepper` has no `position` rule at all (styles.css:195) — adding `position: sticky; top: var(--chrome-h)` and compacting to 44px is the cheapest possible answer to her loudest complaint and touches zero TypeScript and zero test selectors. This is the single highest value-per-line change in any proposal. (2) Its question numbering is the only data-derived one: the numeric tail of the rubric id. I verified this IS Dan's `sheetRef` and IS continuous down a domain — Business runs BU-Q1..BU-Q14, then BU-Q15..BU-Q27, through BU-Q61. So the gutter number, the id chip and Dan's workbook all agree, with no second address invented. (3) `wrap.style.setProperty('--edge', 'var(--s7)')` is valid CSS and reuses the existing eleven tokens with none added. (4) It names the Ctrl+F loss out loud instead of building machinery for it.

DEFECTS: (1) It adds a `ResizeObserver` on `.chrome` and `.stepper` with no guard and never mentions jsdom. `ResizeObserver` is undefined in jsdom 29.1.1 — confirmed — so `new ResizeObserver(...)` inside `paint()` throws a ReferenceError and every assertion in the 325-line suite fails on the first run. (2) Its narrowed repaint splits into `question()` / `rollup()` / `gate()`, and score clicks call only the first two. `rollup()`'s stated targets include the footer's count sentence but not the Save button's `disabled` state, and nothing re-checks `markingProblems`. Since a score alone flips `hasContent`, scoring first in a fresh file leaves Save clickable — a regression in the one hard rule Dan asked for, and one the existing suite would not catch because it types the initiative name before scoring. (3) It calls `sec.scrollIntoView()` on rail clicks; undefined in jsdom, on an untested path today but a trap for the next test. (4) One section open at a time turns the suite's 176-question walk into clicks on hidden nodes. (5) Three sticky tiers plus a 15rem rail needing 1100px means two layouts to maintain.

scores.lens: Progressive disclosure, as a workbook (21 stops)
scores.note:
Contains the single best product insight in the whole set, wrapped in the most fragile machinery.

THE INSIGHT: two progress bars, because one bar over 176 questions moves 0.57% per answer and nobody can see that, while a section bar over a 9-question median moves 11%. She asked for progress that is always seen AND an animation when she finishes a question. An animation needs something visible to move, and this is the only proposal that does the arithmetic and concludes the reward belongs on the section bar. Also strong: keeping process colour (grey to green) separate from Dan's ramp, with the explicit argument that a score of 1 must not paint the card edge dark red because that reads as a form error — a problem the winner actually has. And the per-section forward button naming its destination, replacing a pager that currently sits 20,000px down the page.

WHY IT LOSES: (1) `hidden="until-found"` plus a `beforematch` listener that repaints is fragile in a way it does not flag — the handler tears down and rebuilds the element the browser is mid-way through revealing, so the found match is lost. That is real machinery for a secondary benefit, against "i also dont wanna overcomplicate it". (2) It sets `--chrome-h` with a `ResizeObserver` and calls the JSDOM failure harmless. An unguarded `new ResizeObserver` does not fall back to the CSS default, it throws. (3) It claims "no edits needed" for test/ui.mjs, which is technically true — hidden nodes are still queryable and clickable in jsdom, confirmed — but it means the 176-question walk silently becomes a walk over nodes a real user cannot reach, and it does not say so. (4) Question numbers are position-within-section, so section 2 question 3 is numbered 3 while Dan calls it Q17: a third address. (5) 124px chrome plus a 96px two-bar footer, three sticky bands below 1000px, and a per-question drawer that puts "Why that score" one click away 176 times.

The most compression and the best print thinking; also the largest departure from what is already there and from what she said she wanted.

GENUINELY BEST AT: (1) Print. `content: attr(data-print)` on the score cell prints the answer with no extra node, which fixes the fact that scores do not print at all today (`button { display: none !important }`, styles.css:553). And it is the only proposal to catch that a 2-row textarea clips its own content when printed, so justification and evidence values must be mirrored into print-only paragraphs on `input` rather than `change`. (2) jsdom discipline, mostly right: it guards IO citing jsdom 29.1.1 and keeps every reduced-motion branch in CSS because `matchMedia` is absent — both confirmed. (3) The reasoned rejection of a real `<table>`: table navigation mode intercepts the arrow keys the score row needs. Correct, and the right call. (4) Landing the completion reward on a pinned element (the section chip in the frozen bar) so it is visible however deep you are. (5) `--band` / `--gutter` as lightness steps rather than hue steps, so row separation survives greyscale and print.

WHY IT LOSES: (1) It deletes the per-question ladder — 176 copies — reversing a decision the source documents in a comment: "The ladder, shown rather than hidden. It is the guidance, not just the scale." Its replacement is a `mouseover`/`focusin` hint, which is dead on touch and new code. (2) It moves the primary navigation into `.sticky-footer`, i.e. last in DOM order after 61 questions. That is an accessibility regression against today, where the stepper is at the top, and it is unaddressed. (3) The 62px bottom-chrome budget is optimistic: `.footer-inner` is `flex-wrap: wrap`, and five 6.4rem tabs plus a 9rem track plus a pill plus two buttons will wrap to two rows on a 1366-wide laptop. (4) 26px × 27.6px score segments, clicked 176 times, sit right at the WCAG 2.2 floor with no headroom. (5) Five test edits, the largest churn, one of which (`Symbiotic` moving from the question to `view()`) encodes a removed feature. (6) It admits the metaphor over-promises — sheet tabs imply rename, reorder, add, none of which exist. She values conventions over invention, and importing a spreadsheet's furniture into a web form is invention wearing a convention's clothes.

verdicts.winner: The assessment as a published standard (numbered outline + persistent TOC rail) — proposal 4
grafts: Graft proposal 1's sticky stepper wholesale and drop proposal 4's vertical rail stepper. `.stepper` has no `position` rule today (styles.css:195), so `position: sticky; top: var(--chrome-h); z-index: 28; background: var(--bg)` plus compacting `.step` to a one-line 44px row is a CSS-only change touching zero TypeScript and zero test selectors. It is the literal answer to "like in Excel, they would always be seen" — a pinned horizontal row of five tabs with per-tab progress. Keep proposal 4's left rail, but scope it to SECTIONS only.

Replace proposal 4's invented 1.1.4 numbering with proposal 1's: the numeric tail of the rubric id, parsed `/(\d+)$/` with a running-index fallback. I verified this is exactly Dan's `sheetRef` and is continuous down a domain (Business: BU-Q1..Q14, BU-Q15..Q27, … BU-Q61), so the gutter number, the `.qid` chip and Dan's workbook all agree and there is one address per question instead of two.

Graft proposal 3's section-level progress bar onto proposal 4's segmented overall bar. 1/176 = 0.57% is invisible; the median section is 9 questions, so a section bar moves 11% per answer. The completion animation belongs on the bar that visibly moves — that is what "make it sparkly … animation when you finish a question" actually requires.

Take proposal 3's rule that process colour and score colour stay separate: grey-to-green for answered/not-answered, Dan's `--s0..--s10` ramp only for what the score means. Proposal 4 currently puts `t1` on the `.q-ans` left edge, so a score of 1 paints a dark-red edge that reads as a form error. Fix that before building it.

Take proposal 2's print mechanics: `content: attr(data-print)` on the score cell, written by the existing `paintChosen` closure, and mirror the justification and evidence field values into print-only `

` elements on `input` (not `change`). A 2-row textarea clips its own content when printed, which no other proposal caught, and today the score does not print at all.

Add proposal 1's `scroll-margin-top: calc(var(--chrome-h) + …)` on `.question`, `.card.section`, `textarea`, `.score-row` and `.evidence`. Browsers honour `scroll-margin` for sequential-focus scrolling, not only `scrollIntoView`, and Tab landing under a pinned header is the known failure mode of every sticky design here.

Use proposal 1's `--edge` technique for the per-question status colour: `wrap.style.setProperty('--edge', `var(--s${v})`)` with `background: var(--edge, var(--accent))`. Valid CSS, reuses the eleven existing tokens, adds none.

Adopt proposal 1's stale-readout test: after a score change AND after an n/a toggle, assert every readout agrees. The n/a case is the one where the denominator moves (`SectionScore.total` counts not-n/a), and it is the likeliest place a hand-patched counter goes silently stale under a narrowed repaint.

Take the resume cursor, but put it where proposals 2 and 3 put it, not where proposal 1 does: a separate `gc-arch-assessment:view` localStorage key, keyed with the rubric version and with section keys namespaced `${domainId}/${sectionId}` (section ids repeat — `defining-the-current-state` exists in all four domains). Interface state should not ride inside the JSON file emailed to TBS.

Add proposal 3's per-section forward control at the foot of each section, naming its destination ("Next: 1.2 Defining the Business Solution"). `pager()` currently sits ~20,000px down the page and offers no route onward from the last domain.

Adopt proposal 3's default for any folded block: render it open when it already has content (`ans.justification` non-empty or `ans.evidence.length > 0`), closed otherwise. Correct default even if the drawer itself is not built.

Land the section-completion reward on a PINNED element, as proposal 2 does — the sticky section header or the rail row — so the reward is visible however far down the page she is. A flourish 4,000px above the fold is a flourish nobody sees.
Keep proposal 2's `--band` / `--gutter` tokens as lightness steps rather than hue steps if any row banding is used, so the separation survives greyscale, print and every form of colour blindness.

Non-negotiable environment guards, drawn from proposals 2 and 4 and confirmed by probing jsdom 29.1.1 directly: no `IntersectionObserver`, no `ResizeObserver`, no `matchMedia`, no `Element.scrollIntoView`, and `getBoundingClientRect()` returns all zeros. So: guard IO with `typeof IntersectionObserver === 'function'` and `disconnect()` before re-observing (`renderSubmit` runs on every paint, or the observers accumulate); never use `ResizeObserver` unguarded (proposals 1 and 3 both would throw and take the whole suite down); guard any measured height with `if (h > 0)`; navigate with real anchors, not `scrollIntoView`; and keep every `prefers-reduced-motion` branch in CSS with no TypeScript `matchMedia` test.

Whatever narrowed-repaint shape is built, keep the gate valve proposals 3 and 4 both specify: compare `markingProblems(a).length` (or `canSave(a)`) before and after, and fall back to the full `repaintApp()` when it flips. `hasContent` in marking.ts includes `typeof ans.score === 'number'`, so the first score in a fresh file arms the save gate. Without the valve, Save stays clickable on an unmarked file — a regression in the one hard rule Dan asked for, and one the current suite will not catch because it types the initiative name before it scores.
verdicts.reasoning:
All four proposals converge on the same five moves — pin the domain tabs, put the section list somewhere permanent, give the question a card or row with a number and a status glyph, add an always-visible progress bar with a one-shot completion animation, and narrow the repaint so a score click stops rebuilding 4,049 nodes. That convergence is itself evidence the diagnosis is right. So the ranking is decided almost entirely by implementation reality, which is what I was asked to judge on.

I probed the actual environment rather than trusting any proposal's claims. jsdom 29.1.1, which `npm run test:ui` drives, has no IntersectionObserver, no ResizeObserver, no matchMedia, no `Element.scrollIntoView`, and `getBoundingClientRect()` returns all zeros. That one fact separates the field: proposal 4 names and guards every one of those traps, proposal 2 guards most of them, and proposals 1 and 3 both add an unguarded `ResizeObserver` inside `paint()` — a ReferenceError that takes down all 100-plus assertions on the first run. Proposal 1 never mentions jsdom at all despite the suite living there.

The second decider is the marking gate. `markingProblems()` treats a bare score as content (`typeof ans.score === 'number'`), so the first score in a fresh file is what arms the save gate. Once the repaint is narrowed, that transition has to be re-checked explicitly or the Save button goes stale and an unmarked Protected B file becomes saveable. Proposals 3 and 4 both specify the check and fall back to a full repaint when it flips. Proposals 1 and 2 do not — and the existing suite would not catch it, because it types the initiative name before it scores, so it would ship as a live defect in the one rule Dan asked to be a hard gate.

Proposal 4 wins on care shown per line of the existing codebase. It is the only one that catches why `<li>`-wrapping the stepper would break `.step.complete:not(:first-child)`; the only one that dual-classes the question node specifically to avoid a test rename; the only one that notices its own new section-toggle buttons would be hidden by the existing `button { display: none !important }` print rule; the only one that catches `.card { page-break-inside: avoid }` fighting a 4,400px section card; and the only one that defaults every section open, so the suite's 176-question walk stays a walk over reachable nodes rather than over hidden ones. Its inversion of the evidence tint is also the sharpest design read in the set — `.evidence` really is the only tinted block inside a question today, which is precisely why it reads louder than the question she is trying to answer.

What proposal 4 gets wrong is answerable by grafting, which is why the grafts list is long and specific. It does not shorten the page; it answers the Excel remark with a vertical list in a margin rather than a pinned row of tabs; it invents a second question address beside Dan's own; and it colours the status edge with the maturity ramp, so a score of 1 paints a dark-red edge that reads as an error in the form. Proposal 1 supplies the fix for two of those at almost no cost — its sticky stepper is a CSS-only change on unchanged DOM, and its gutter number is Dan's own `sheetRef`, which I confirmed runs continuously down each domain. Proposal 3 supplies the fix for the other two: the section-level bar that actually moves 11% per answer instead of 0.57%, and the rule that process colour and score colour must stay apart.

Proposal 2 is the most interesting failure. It compresses the page five-fold and thinks hardest about print. But it deletes 176 copies of the ladder, reversing a decision the source explicitly defends in a comment; it moves the primary navigation to last in DOM order, after 61 questions; its 62px footer budget will wrap on a 1366-wide laptop because `.footer-inner` already wraps; and it admits its own metaphor over-promises. For a user who values conventions over invention and said plainly that she does not want it overcomplicated, importing a spreadsheet's furniture into a government web form is the most invention on offer, dressed as the most convention.

scores.lens: Progressive disclosure as a workbook (21 stops, section rail, two footer bars)
scores.note: Cleanest against every stated axis and the only one that introduces no new SC risk. It is the only proposal with a skip link (2.4.1), and it names why: five domain tabs plus six rail rows in front of the questions on every navigation. Its print unfold is the only mechanism in the set that actually works — `.qsection[hidden] { display: block !important; content-visibility: visible }` overriding the `hidden` attribute, PLUS beforeprint/afterprint, and it names Safari firing neither. It also removes the need for a print-only score mechanism entirely by putting the answer in a visible `.q-verdict` pill in the question header: present as text, in reading order, for screen readers, for print, with nothing to go stale. Focus is moved to `h2.sechead-title[tabindex=-1]` on navigation with a live-region announcement; the live region is scoped to section changes with an explicit argument against 176 announcements. Best reasoning on semantic colour in the set: process colour (green/grey rail, check glyph) is kept strictly apart from Dan's ramp, because a score of 1 painting the card edge dark red reads as a form error. Real h1/h2/h3 outline where today 61 questions sit under one h2. Reduced motion keeps the check drawn (`stroke-dashoffset: 0`). Costs: the heaviest sticky stack once the rail collapses below 1000px — chrome ~124 plus a 44px rail strip plus a newly sticky section header plus a 96px two-bar footer, which at 320x568 is roughly half the viewport, and it has no `max-height` rule to shed a tier; 250px rail is px not rem; find-in-page and printing are domain-scoped (4 print jobs); and its own `details.q-more` drawer is not covered by its print unfold if a user closes it manually.

scores.lens: The assessment as a published standard (numbered outline, TOC rail, hanging numbers)
scores.note: The deepest print craft in the set, including two things nobody else caught: `button:not(.sec-toggle) { display: none !important }`, because today's blanket `button` hide would delete any section title placed inside a toggle, and `.sec-head { position: static !important }` because Chrome has duplicated stuck sticky headers onto every printed page. It correctly replaces `.card { page-break-inside: avoid }` with `auto` and moves `avoid` down to the question, kills the tinted `.q-ans` slab with `background: none !important`, hides `.ladder-box` (~40 pages), unhides `.marking-banner.print-only`, and is the only one to print all three answer states explicitly — "Score 7 of 10 — Scalable & Secure" / "Not applicable" / "Not answered" — so an unanswered question prints a stated absence rather than a blank. Also the only proposal to notice the existing `nav.path` has no accessible name, and to reason that a second `<nav>` without one makes a screen reader read "navigation, navigation". Three question states are three glyph *shapes*, not three colours. `tabindex="-1"` on the jump target with the correct reason. Guards IntersectionObserver and is the only one to name the observer leak. Sharpest test-preservation catch in the set: keeping `nav.stepper`'s buttons as direct children because `<li>` wrappers break `.step.complete:not(:first-child)` — and a dead suite is how an a11y regression ships. Two real penalties: it ships a persisted collapse state and a bulk "Collapse answered sections" button but adds **no print rule to unhide a collapsed `.sec-body`**, so the documented path is collapse-then-print-and-lose-the-prose; and it has the heaviest 320px furniture of the four — chrome plus a ~110px rail strip plus a sticky section head plus an uncompacted 90px footer is over half a 568px viewport. It also inherits the clipped `rows=2` textarea in print without mirroring it.

scores.lens: Long-form government survey instrument (numbered form, permanent left rail)
scores.note: The best keyboard and screen-reader work in the set, and the best small-viewport budget — then it loses on the one thing the brief penalises hardest. Unique wins: it is the only proposal that handles where the tab stop goes when the whole radiogroup is disabled by Not applicable (all eleven get `aria-disabled` and `disabled`, the row's stop moves to the checkbox); it is the only one to put `scroll-margin-top` on the focusable *descendants* — `textarea`, `.score-row`, `.evidence` — not just the jump targets, which is the actual fix for Tab landing under a pinned header; the 600ms-debounced polite live region with count-only text is the right discipline over 176 questions; it names older JAWS announcing `<details>` state inconsistently and carries the state independently in `aria-current` and the live region; it takes the score pill out of the `h2` so it stops reading "Business Architecture 5.2"; and it is alone in noting that at `#191c22` on `#21252d` the dark-mode nesting is nearly invisible, so every level also carries a 1px border. It also spends the sticky budget most carefully: a 4px strip inside the existing `.chrome` rather than a new tier, a footer compacted to ~46px, and a real `max-height: 800px` rule that drops the sticky section header outright, with that header named as the designated first cut. The fatal problem: the design is one-section-open-at-a-time inside `<details>`, and its stated print mitigation is `details { display: block }` — which does not open a closed `<details>` in Blink or WebKit. There is no `beforeprint`. So a printed Business Architecture carries roughly 9 of 61 questions, and since the results table has no justification column, five sixths of the submitter's prose prints from nowhere at all. It leans on the same false mechanism a second time, as the mitigation for losing Ctrl+F across the domain. One line of `beforeprint` would fix it, but as written the brief's top penalty lands squarely, twice. Minor: it claims both that the footer's duplicate pill is dropped to reach 46px and that `.footer-score .pill` stays for the test.

scores.lens: Spreadsheet chrome without the grid (sheet tabs, frozen header, row-per-question)
scores.note:
Best print *engineering* and the best-argued single a11y decision in the set, undone by three regressions that are core to the metaphor rather than incidental. It is the only proposal that fixes the clipped-textarea print defect: the justification is mirrored into a `

` on **`input`**, not `change`, so prose typed and printed without leaving the field still prints, with `.has-content` gating so empty drawers don't print — and this matters more than it realises, because the results table has no justification column. `content: attr(data-print)` prints the score with no extra node. `.drawer[hidden] { display: block !important }` correctly overrides the `hidden` attribute rather than fighting `

`. The rejection of a real `` is the sharpest reasoning in the whole set and is correct: table navigation mode intercepts the arrow keys the score row needs, and eleven buttons in one cell get the column header re-announced on every focus move. `cssId()` plus `${domain.id}--${section.id}` namespacing is the only place the verified four-way `defining-the-current-state` collision is handled with a sanitiser. Its two new neutrals are explicitly a lightness step and not a hue step, so the banding survives greyscale. Lowest tab-stop count (about 185 per domain). Against that: at 320px the 11-segment strip spans roughly 242px, giving ~22px targets — under its own stated 24px floor and under 2.5.8; the per-question ladder is deleted in favour of a hint shown on `mouseover`/`focusin` that can sit up to 61 rows from the control, which is hover-only guidance with no 1.4.13 dismissable/persistent handling and nothing at all for touch; its section chips are real anchors but get no `tabindex="-1"` on the target, so Tab after a jump returns to the chip strip; there is no skip link and no live region; and a five-column row grid with 29.4rem of fixed columns rides on a single 720px breakpoint, which is precisely the width band a 200% zoom lands in. Its own honest figure — 242px of sticky furniture on a 667px phone — has no `max-height` rule behind it.

verdicts.winner: Progressive disclosure as a workbook (21 stops, section rail, two footer bars)
grafts: From the published-standard proposal, the whole print block, verbatim: `button:not(.sec-toggle) { display: none !important }` (today's blanket `button` hide is what deletes a title placed inside a toggle), `.sec-head { position: static !important; break-after: avoid }` (Chrome has duplicated stuck sticky headers onto every printed page), `.card { break-inside: auto }` replacing today's `avoid` with `avoid` moved down to the question, and `.q-ans { background: none !important }` so a tinted answer panel does not print as a grey slab.

From the published-standard proposal, print all three answer states as words — "Score 7 of 10 — Scalable & Secure", "Not applicable", "Not answered" — so an unanswered question prints a stated absence instead of a blank where its answer belongs.

From the spreadsheet proposal, mirror the justification textarea into a print-visible `

` on `input` (not `change`), gated by a `.has-content` class. This is not optional polish: `rows=2` clips in print, and `table.detail` on the results page has no justification column, so the submit view is the only place the submitter's own words print at all.
From the spreadsheet proposal, `content: attr(data-print)` on the score cell — prints the answer with no extra node and no second source of truth.

From the spreadsheet proposal, a `cssId()` sanitiser plus `${domain.id}--${section.id}` namespacing for every id, anchor and `aria-controls`. I verified `defining-the-current-state` appears four times in the rubric; any scheme keyed on section ids collides today, and the published-standard proposal is right that a stale key will strand sections in the wrong state for an afternoon.

From the survey-instrument proposal, the disabled-radiogroup tab stop: when Not applicable is ticked, set `aria-disabled` on all eleven buttons and move the row's single tab stop to the checkbox. No other proposal says where focus goes when the group it owns is entirely disabled.

From the survey-instrument proposal, put `scroll-margin-top: calc(--chrome-h + …)` on the focusable descendants — `textarea`, `.score-row`, `.evidence` — not only on the section jump targets. Browsers honour `scroll-margin` for focus scrolling, and this is the actual fix for Tab landing under the pinned stack.

From the survey-instrument proposal, its sticky-budget discipline: put the overall progress strip inside the existing `.chrome` block rather than opening a new tier, compact the footer to one ~46px row, and add a `@media (max-height: 800px)` rule that drops the sticky section header outright. The winner's stack — chrome ~124 plus a 44px rail strip plus a sticky section header plus a 96px two-bar footer — is about half of a 568px viewport and roughly 60% at 200% zoom, and it has no rule to shed a tier. Under that rule, drop to the section bar alone in the footer.

From the survey-instrument proposal, the 600ms-debounced polite live region carrying only the count plus a section-complete sentence, and the note that older JAWS announces `<details>` state inconsistently so the state must also live in `aria-current`.

From the survey-instrument and published-standard proposals, take the score pill out of the domain heading (with an `.sr-only` " out of 10" beside it) so it stops reading as "Business Architecture 5.2".
From the published-standard proposal, give the new rail `<nav>` an `aria-label` and fix the existing unlabelled `nav.path` in the same pass, or a screen reader reads "navigation, navigation".

From the published-standard proposal, three glyph shapes for the three question states — dashed empty circle, check, en dash — rather than three colours; and add a `✓` to the domain and section counts, which would otherwise be complete-by-hue on the bars alone.

From the spreadsheet proposal, replace the horizontal chip strip with a native `<select>` below ~700px whose `onchange` sets `location.hash`. It is the best 320px navigation pattern of the four, it is one line tall, and it is keyboard and screen-reader native.
From the spreadsheet proposal, two new neutrals defined as a lightness step and not a hue step, so any banding or gutter tint survives greyscale and every form of colour vision deficiency.

From the spreadsheet proposal, record its `<table>`-versus-list argument in a comment: the questionnaire is a list that looks like a sheet because table navigation mode intercepts the arrow keys the score row needs. It is the reason not to revisit this later.

From the spreadsheet and published-standard proposals, guard `IntersectionObserver` with `typeof IntersectionObserver === 'function'`, disconnect the previous set at the top of each paint (20 observers per paint otherwise accumulate), and keep the reduced-motion opt-out entirely in CSS — jsdom has neither `IntersectionObserver` nor `matchMedia`, and `npm run test:ui` throws on load.

From the published-standard proposal, keep `nav.stepper`'s five buttons as direct children rather than wrapping them in `<li>`, or `.step.complete:not(:first-child)` breaks. A dead test suite is how the next accessibility regression ships unnoticed.

Delete `details { display: block }` as a print mechanism wherever it appears, including from the current stylesheet. It does not open a closed `<details>` in Blink or WebKit; it is why section titles vanish from print today, and it is the false premise the survey-instrument proposal builds its accordion on. Anything foldable that must print should use the `hidden` attribute and a `[hidden] { display: block !important }` override, plus `beforeprint`/`afterprint` for Safari — which is the winner's own mechanism, and it should be extended to cover its `details.q-more` drawer, not just `.qsection[hidden]`.
verdicts.reasoning:
Judged only on accessibility, keyboard, screen readers, print, 320px and 200% zoom, the field separates on two things: whether the fold loses content when printed, and how much of a short viewport the sticky furniture eats.

On print, the stakes are higher than any proposal except the spreadsheet one realises. `table.detail` on the results page carries `# / Question / Score / Weight / Evidence` and no justification column, so the submitter's prose prints from the submit view or nowhere. That turns "content behind a fold" into content loss.

That is what disqualifies the survey-instrument proposal, which otherwise has the deepest keyboard and screen-reader work in the set and the most careful sticky budget. Its design is one-section-open-at-a-time inside `<details>`, and its stated print mitigation is `details { display: block }`, which does not open a closed `<details>` in Blink or WebKit — it is the same cargo cult already in the stylesheet, and the reason section titles do not print today. There is no `beforeprint`. A printed Business Architecture would carry about 9 of 61 questions, and it leans on the same false mechanism a second time as the mitigation for losing Ctrl+F. One line would fix it, but the brief's sharpest penalty lands twice.

The published-standard proposal has the best print craft of the four — the Chrome sticky-header duplication, the `button:not(.sec-toggle)` catch, moving `break-inside: avoid` down to the question, all three answer states printed as words — and the best incidental catches (the unlabelled existing `nav.path`, the observer leak, the `<li>` wrapper that would break the test). But it ships a persisted collapse state and a bulk "Collapse answered sections" button with no print rule to unhide a collapsed `.sec-body`, so it builds the documented path to the exact failure it otherwise guards against, and it has the heaviest 320px furniture in the set.

The spreadsheet proposal has the best print engineering (the textarea mirrored on `input` is the only fix in the set for the clipped `rows=2`) and the best-argued single decision (list over table, because table mode intercepts the arrow keys the score row needs). But its regressions are structural rather than incidental: ~22px score segments at 320px, under its own stated floor; the per-question ladder replaced by a hover/focus hint up to 61 rows from the control, with no 1.4.13 handling and nothing for touch; anchors with no `tabindex="-1"` on the target; no skip link, no live region, no short-viewport rule; and a five-column grid with 29.4rem of fixed columns on a single 720px breakpoint, which is exactly where a 200% zoom lands.

The workbook proposal wins because it is the only one that introduces no new failure on any axis I was asked to judge. It is the only one with a skip link, and it names the reason. Its print unfold is the only mechanism that actually works — overriding the `hidden` attribute, plus `beforeprint`/`afterprint`, plus the note that Safari fires neither. And it makes the score a visible `.q-verdict` pill in the question header rather than a print-only node, so the answer is in reading order for screen readers, in the printout, and in a glance down the page, with no second source of truth to go stale. Its reasoning on colour is the best in the set: process state and Dan's maturity ramp are kept strictly apart, because a score of 1 painting the card edge dark red reads as a form error rather than a low score.

Its real cost is the one the brief also penalises: once the rail collapses below 1000px it stacks chrome, a rail strip, a newly sticky section header and a 96px two-bar footer, which is about half a 320x568 viewport and worse at 200% zoom, and it has no `max-height` rule to shed a tier. That is a bounded, mechanical fix, and the survey-instrument proposal's budget discipline is sitting right there to graft in — which is the opposite of the survey-instrument proposal's problem, where the flaw is the navigation model itself. Two further notes for the winner: its 250px rail is px, not rem, and its own `details.q-more` drawer is not covered by its print unfold if someone closes it by hand.

One finding that applies to all four: `.topbar` is `flex-wrap: wrap`, so at 320px it becomes two rows and the chrome is nearer 117px than 86px. Every sticky budget in every proposal understates the narrow case, and every one of them should be measured with `--chrome-h` rather than trusted from the desktop figure.

audience.recommendation:
Keep one file and one build. Split the app into two sides at the level of the header: a submitter side, which is what the file opens as, and an assessor side reached by one plainly worded door on the Start page and by the URL index.html#assessor. Each side carries its own path in the header, and neither side's path names the other side's work. Nobody is asked to pick a role, and a submitter never has to know the assessor side exists.

Turn down the other three. Two builds buys you about twenty lines of code and costs you distribution and version drift. A mode chosen on first run puts a question in front of hundreds of people when a handful of them have a non-default answer. A hidden entry as the only route means the two assessors who need it phone you when they forget the trick.

The door is visible, so it needs no support call. The path is per-side, so the two jobs never appear side by side again. That is her Eventbrite analogy honoured without two apps to maintain.
audience.mechanism:
All of it fits in main.ts, which already holds the shell, the header and the mode variable.

- `type Side = 'submit' | 'assess'`, and `let side: Side = 'submit'`. The existing `Mode` splits along it: home, submit and results belong to the submitter, review belongs to the assessor, settings belongs to neither.
- At boot, read `location.hash === '#assessor'` first, then a localStorage key, wrapped in try/catch the same way `autosave` and `loadDraft` already are. When storage is blocked the default is the submitter side, which is the correct default for the majority.
- `header()` builds `nav.path` from `side`. The `.path`, `.tab` and `.chev` styles already exist, so the markup shape does not change.
- One function does the switch. `goSide(next)` sets `side`, writes the storage key, sets `location.hash`, sets `mode` to that side's home, paints, scrolls to top. Setting a hash on a file:// URL does not reload the page.
- Clicking the brand goes to the current side's home: the Start page for a submitter, the submissions list for an assessor.
- The Start page gains one line under the hero: "Reviewing submissions for TBS? Open the assessor side." It uses the existing `.linkish` style and it lives outside `nav.path`, so it reads as a different door.
- The assessor side names itself with a word. A bordered ASSESSOR chip beside the brand, built from the existing `.marking-inline` primitive, plus a "Leave the assessor side" item at the end of the path. The word carries the signal, so there is no colour-only tell.
- While `header()` is open, add `aria-current="page"` to the active tab and an `aria-label` to `nav.path`. Two lines, and it closes a real screen-reader gap in the current build.
- Print needs no change. The topbar is already `display:none` in print, and each side's printed artefact names itself: the submitter prints an assessment carrying its initiative name and its marking, the assessor prints the one-pager carrying the initiative and the reviewer's name.
- views-submit.ts, views-review.ts, views-results.ts, scoring.ts, flags.ts and the rubric are untouched.

Write one sentence in the README before anyone asks it in a meeting: the divider is a workspace divider and it is not access control. The assessor side reads only files the person already holds, the CSP blocks every outbound request from both sides, and anyone who reaches #assessor sees an empty dropzone.
audience.whyNotTwoApps:
Against, and the reason is distribution.

1. The code saving is real and small. An esbuild `define`, a second entry file and a second output in build.mjs, around twenty lines. The cost falls somewhere else.
2. One file is the whole trust story in the README: email it, put it on a USB stick, host it, the behaviour is identical. Two files means two artefacts, two version numbers loose in departments, two sets of instructions and two published URLs.
3. scoring.ts is shared by both sides. Two builds means two copies of the scorer in the wild, and an assessor can audit a submission with a build that computes a different number from the one the submitter saw. The README already names version drift as the reason every assessment records the rubric version it was answered against. Two builds doubles that surface.
4. test/ui.mjs drives one built file end to end: it fills in all 176 questions, saves the file, and loads it back through the assessor side in the same page. That single test is where this project's quality lives. Two builds either breaks it or forces two JSDOM instances passing a blob between them.
5. One person needs both sides in the same hour: you demonstrating, Dan trying it, an assessor checking which question a submitter saw. Today that is one click.

Keep two builds as an option you have not exercised. The `side` variable is the seam, so if a department ever demands an assessor-free file, the change is an hour's work and reversible.
audience.navigationChange:
Submitter side, the default: **Start > Fill it in > My results**. Three steps, one job. Same width as today's path, so no new wrapping on a narrow screen.

Assessor side: **Submissions**, with the ASSESSOR chip beside the brand and "Leave the assessor side" at the end of the path.

The gear stays at the far right on both sides, because Settings belongs to neither.

Where "See my results" belongs: on the submitter's path, as the third step, visible from every screen a submitter can reach. The buttons you already have stay, since the sticky footer and the pager are the action at the point of finishing. The header item is the always-visible way there, and the way back. It also closes a gap: today the only exit from the results page is a button underneath everything else, and the questionnaire's own "See my results" is a button roughly 20,000px down the Business page.

What goes away: "Review submissions" as a tab. That is the one string test/ui.mjs clicks to reach the assessor side.

What I would leave alone for now: a breadcrumb reading Submissions > initiative name when a submission is open. It reads well, but `openDetail()` paints into root without going through `paint()`, so the header would go stale. Making it live means routing the assessor's list and detail through the shell, which is a bigger change than the header itself. Keep Submissions as one step and keep the existing "Back to the list" button.

Files under /Users/maryy/Desktop/Claude Hub/Claude -- TBS/TBS fall/Self-assessment tool/

- src/main.ts, the bulk: the `Side` type, the variable, `goSide()`, `header()` rebuilt around the path, boot reading hash and storage, one line on the Start page, the chip. Roughly 60 to 70 lines changed in a 294-line file.
- src/styles.css: about 10 lines. A chip class, or reuse `.marking-inline`. `.path`, `.tab` and `.chev` need nothing.

- README.md: a short section on the two sides, carrying the line that says the divider is not access control.
- Untouched: views-submit.ts, views-review.ts, views-results.ts, scoring.ts, flags.ts, rubric.ts, marking.ts, dom.ts, the rubric JSON, build.mjs, template.html.

Half a day, including the test update. No new dependency, no new file, no change to the built output's size or its CSP.
audience.risks:
- A remembered side stranding a submitter. You demonstrate the assessor side on a shared laptop, the next person opens the file and gets a dropzone. The exit is always in the header and its label names where it goes. Test this exact case before you show it.
- Somebody calls the divider security. Say in the README that it is not, before the question arrives in a meeting. In a Protected B conversation that answer has to be on the record and unambiguous.
- Nick and Allison cannot find the door on day one. Hand them the #assessor URL directly and let the Start page line be the backup.
- localStorage blocked in a locked-down profile on file://. The side is then not remembered, and the assessor clicks once per session or uses the hash. The failure mode leaves everyone else on the correct default.

audience.recommendation:
Separate them, but by one variable in main.ts, and only as part of the navigation fix she already asked for.

The verdict: add a role to main.ts, default it to submitter, and let it choose which destinations the header offers. Do not produce two builds. The whole distribution story is one file that can be emailed, dropped on a share, or opened from a USB stick, and a second file breaks that story for a gain I measured at 10.7 KB.

The counterweight she deserves to hear first: role confusion is nowhere in her five complaints. All five are inside the questionnaire. The loudest is that the domain tabs disappear after 174 pixels of a 20,190-pixel page, and that one is fixed by moving nav.stepper inside div.chrome, which is already position: sticky; top: 0. A child of a sticky parent pins with the parent, so the relocated stepper needs no position rule of its own. One move in renderSubmit, one selector kept, complaint three closed. If only one thing gets done this week, it is that, and it is four lines.

Which is why the role split earns its place rather than a slot of its own. Pinning the stepper costs vertical space, and space is the thing this page has none of. The chrome is 86 pixels today (topbar 59, marking banner 27). Adding the 70-pixel stepper makes it 156, and against the 100-pixel sticky footer the usable band at 900 pixels falls from 714 to 644. 714 already held exactly one question mid-scroll. So the pinned strip has to be compact, and the top row has to surrender a destination to pay for the row beneath it. The destination to surrender is "Review submissions", because the person answering 176 questions will never press it. The navigation fix and the role split are the same edit, and doing them apart costs more than doing them together.

The minimum version of separation is therefore: one build, one URL, one artifact, and a role that decides which header the person gets.
audience.whyNotTwoApps:
I built both halves in a scratch copy of the real source to check, so these are esbuild numbers, not estimates.

  current build, both roles                                113.6 KB
  submitter only, renderReview and its tab removed         102.9 KB
  assessor only, renderSubmit and renderResults removed     95.3 KB

Four arguments against two builds.

The weight saving is not there. Dropping the entire assessor side saves the submitter 10.7 KB, 9.4 percent. views-review.ts is 18.5 KB of source, but the expensive parts are shared and stay in both: the rubric at 38.4 KB minified, styles.css at 29.0 KB, and 36.3 KB of model code (scoring, flags, marking, types, storage, csv, attach, dom, rubric) that both roles need in full. Two builds total 198.2 KB against 113.6 KB, so separating produces 74 percent more bytes to publish for a tool whose one virtue is being a single file.

What the two sides share is not rendering. It is the flag engine, and sharing it is the product. views-results.ts (9.3 KB) and views-review.ts (18.5 KB) are genuinely different code; their only overlap is CSS classes (.card, .headline, .bigscore, .flag, .flag-title, .sev-dot, .challenge, .q-head, .qid, .q-text, .pill, .band, .maturity, .table-wrap) and the model layer, score() and flags() and tone() and csv and marking and attach. The submitter's results page prints "What an assessor will probably ask", and the comment above it gives the reason plainly, that showing this to the submitter removes the ambush. Two builds means two copies of flags.ts, and the first time they drift the submitter is ambushed by the exact thing the design promised she would not be. That is a correctness failure. It is more than a packaging inconvenience.

It deletes the only end-to-end test. test/ui.mjs is one JSDOM document that answers all 176 questions, saves, feeds the captured blob into the assessor dropzone, re-scores one question, saves the audited file, then asserts the self-score of 7 survives alongside the audited score of 4. Two builds turn that into two documents with a synthetic handoff, or it goes away. Removing the round-trip test to tidy the navigation is a poor trade at prototype stage.

The confidentiality argument does not hold. With connect-src 'none' and no server, the assessor view can only read files already on that person's own disk. A submitter looking at the review tab cannot reach anyone else's Protected B material; she would have to already hold it. Separating the builds to keep submitters away from submissions solves a problem the missing network already solved.

One practical cost on top: two filenames create a second version axis with no detector. The app already warns when a saved file's rubric version differs from the running rubric. Nobody will warn Allison that she opened assessment-v3.json in reviewer-v2.html.

Audience check, in her favour: three people, and one of them (Dan) wants both sides. Two builds to serve three people, one of whom needs both, is the wrong shape.
